intro:
By the end of this track you can describe any data system in the terms the rest of the course uses: which data is the system of record and which is derived from it, whether a question is operational or analytical, how fast the system answers (as percentiles, not averages), which faults it survives, what its load is and which extreme of that load breaks it, what its machines share as it grows, and what it costs the people who run it. Along the way you'll size a pool with Little's law, catch a load test that hides stalls, price fan-out on read against fan-out on write, fit a scalability curve to measurements, and turn an SLO into alerts that page only when the error budget is really going.

You need to read Kotlin, and nothing else: no networking, operating-systems or database background. Every lesson starts from a concrete problem at a payments company (merchants, payments, a ledger, a nightly settlement batch) and builds the idea up from there, with real numbers from published systems and incidents. The next two tracks, Computer networking and Operating systems, go one layer down, to the machinery that every number in this track rests on.

The labs are plain Kotlin in the `sim` module, one package per lesson (`sfz.found.l01` to `sfz.found.l06`), and need no Docker. They model each mechanism in memory, and where time matters they use virtual time: a clock the code advances instead of waiting, so a day of traffic or a three-day alert window runs in milliseconds and every test gives the same numbers on every laptop. From the `labs` folder, run `./gradlew :sim:test --tests 'sfz.found.lNN.*'` until it passes; `./gradlew :sim:solutionTest --tests 'sfz.found.lNN.*'` runs the same tests against the reference answers. The Try its run small demos with `./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=<class> --console=plain -q`.
cheatsheet:
## Words this track defines

| Term | Meaning | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| System of record | holds each fact once and wins every disagreement | 1 |
| Derived data | computed from the record (index, cache, materialized view, warehouse, model); can be rebuilt | 1 |
| OLTP, OLAP | a few records by key, in milliseconds, for the application; scans of history, in seconds or minutes, for people | 1 |
| Response time, service time | what the client waits, end to end; the part spent working on the request | 2 |
| Percentile (p99) | 99% of requests are at least this fast; merge histograms, never average percentiles | 2 |
| Coordinated omission | a closed-loop load test that stops sending during a stall, so the stall barely shows | 2 |
| SLO, error budget, burn rate | a target for a measurement over a window; what the target lets fail; how fast that is being spent | 2, 6 |
| Fault, failure | one part breaks; the service misses its SLO | 3 |
| Gray failure | healthy to its own checks, broken for its users | 3 |
| Metastable failure | an overload that the system's own retries keep going after the trigger is gone | 3 |
| Load parameter | a number that drives cost: a rate, a size, a ratio, a count per key | 4 |
| Fan-out on read, on write | build the answer when someone reads; copy each item to every reader when it is written | 4 |
| Shared memory, disk, nothing | what the workers share: RAM; the storage; only the network | 5 |
| COST | the hardware a system needs to beat one competent thread | 5 |
| Essential, accidental complexity | comes from the problem; comes from how it was built | 6 |

## Formulas

```text
mean response time, one worker   S / (1 - utilization)           10 ms of work: 20 ms at 50% busy, 100 ms at 90%
Little's law                     in flight = rate x time         2,000/s x 50 ms = 100 requests in flight
fan-out to N, each slow with p   P(slow) = 1 - (1 - p)^N         p = 1%, N = 100: 63%; N = 200: 87%
Amdahl's law                     1 / (s + (1 - s) / N)           never more than 1 / s
Universal Scalability Law        N / (1 + a(N - 1) + bN(N - 1))  peak at sqrt((1 - a) / b)
push vs pull, per author         posts x followers vs reads x followers: the follower count cancels
celebrity threshold              fan-out writes per second x delivery deadline
error budget                     (1 - SLO) x days x 1,440 minutes
burn rate                        error ratio / (1 - SLO)
budget spent                     burn rate x minutes / (days x 1,440)
dependencies in series           multiply their success rates: 0.999^3 = 99.7%
```

## Numbers worth remembering

| What | Value | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| 99.9%, 99.99%, 99.999% over 30 days | 43.2 min, 4.32 min, 26 s of total outage | 2 |
| Burn-rate alerts for a 30-day SLO | page at 14.4 over 1 h and 5 min (2% of budget); page at 6 over 6 h and 30 min (5%); ticket at 1 over 3 days and 6 h (10%) | 2, 6 |
| Hard-disk failures | 1.36% a year (Backblaze, 2025): 10,000 disks lose one every 2 or 3 days | 3 |
| Catastrophic failures from bad error handling | 92% (Yuan et al., OSDI 2014) | 3 |
| Twitter, 2012 | about 300,000 timeline reads/s, 5,000 tweets/s, 800 entries per timeline; a 31-million-follower tweet took up to 5 minutes | 4 |
| Bluesky, 2025 | a user gets `min(2000 / follows, 1)` of their timeline writes | 4 |
| Largest EC2 instance | 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB of memory (`u7inh-32tb.480xlarge`) | 5 |
| Aurora storage | 10 GB segments, 6 copies in 3 zones, write quorum 4, read quorum 3, repair in about 10 s | 5 |
| COST paper (twitter_rv graph) | union-find on one thread 15 s; label propagation on 128 cores 251 to 1,784 s | 5 |
| AWS cross-zone traffic | $0.02 per GiB, the reason for Kafka's diskless topics (KIP-1150) | 5, 6 |
| 37signals' S3 exit | about $1.5M a year for S3 against $1.5M of arrays plus under $200K a year to run (self-reported) | 6 |

## Questions to ask of any data system

1. Which store is the system of record, and what is derived from it? Could you rebuild every derived copy? (lesson 1)
2. What are p50, p99 and p999, measured at the client by an open-model load test? (lesson 2)
3. Which faults does it survive, are they independent, and what do retries do to it under overload? (lesson 3)
4. What are its load parameters, and which extreme (a celebrity, a heavy follower, a hot merchant) dominates the cost? (lesson 4)
5. What do its machines share, where is the durable copy, and what is only a cache? (lesson 5)
6. Does it beat one good thread on one big machine? (lesson 5)
7. What is its SLO, do its alerts page on burn rate, and can each change be undone? (lesson 6)
recap: A system of record holds each fact once and wins every disagreement; indexes, caches, materialized views and warehouses are derived from it and can be rebuilt. Operational work touches a few records in milliseconds, analytical work scans history.

Response time is service time plus waiting, and waiting explodes as a server nears full utilization. Report percentiles from merged histograms, load-test with an open model, and expect fan-out to make the tail the common case.

A fault is a part breaking; a failure is the service missing its SLO. Hardware faults are routine and mostly independent; software, configuration and human changes are correlated and cause the big outages, and retries can keep an overload going after its trigger is gone.

Describe load by the parameters that drive cost, as distributions. Fan-out on write wins whenever reads outnumber posts, until one celebrity or heavy follower breaks it, so real timelines are hybrids.

Growing past one machine means choosing what to share: memory, disk or nothing. The USL's α says where workers wait and its β what they must keep in agreement; past the peak, more workers make the job slower.
Cloud-native systems separate durable storage (object stores, quorum-replicated log services) from stateless compute with caches, so always ask where the durable copy is.
Measure COST before you distribute: many published systems needed hundreds of cores to beat one thread, and one machine now reaches 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB.

Systems live for years: make them operable (guardrails, runbooks, sane defaults), keep the complexity the problem needs, make changes reversible, and page on error-budget burn rate. Whether to run them yourself depends on how variable the load is and on the skills you have.

quiz.q: A nightly job rebuilds each merchant's daily totals from the payment log into a table the dashboard reads. For one merchant, the totals table and the log disagree. What do you do?
options: Change the log entries to match the totals
Rebuild that merchant's totals from the log
Keep both and show the average
Delete the log entries the totals don't include
quiz.why: The log is the system of record and wins every disagreement; the totals are derived data, and a derived copy that disagrees is stale or wrong. Rebuilding it from the log fixes it. Editing the record to match a derived copy destroys the only trustworthy version.

quiz.q: A service does 10 ms of work per request, with random arrivals and random work times, and runs at 90% utilization. Roughly what mean response time should you expect?
options: 11 ms
19 ms
100 ms
1 s
quiz.why: For one worker the mean response time is S / (1 − ρ) = 10 ms / 0.1 = 100 ms: nine tenths of it is waiting in the queue. 11 ms assumes the 90% only adds a little. 1 s is what you get at 99%.

quiz.q: Two pods of the payment API report p99s of 40 ms and 400 ms, and each served half the requests. What is the p99 of the whole service?
options: 220 ms, the average of the two
400 ms, the worse of the two
40 ms, the better of the two
It can't be worked out from the two p99s; merge the pods' histograms and read the p99 from the merged counts
quiz.why: A percentile depends on the whole distribution. Here only 0.5% of all requests (half of pod B's slowest 1%) are above 400 ms, so the service p99 is below 400 ms, but where depends on both pods' shapes. Averaging percentiles gives a number with no meaning; adding histogram bucket counts and reading the p99 from the total gives the right one.

quiz.q: A configuration file is pushed to the whole fleet, and within a minute every server has crashed. What kind of fault is this, and what is the defence?
options: A correlated configuration fault; roll changes out in stages and have consumers check what they receive
An independent hardware fault; add more replicas
A gray failure; make health checks follow real requests
A metastable failure; add a retry budget
quiz.why: Every server received the same bad input at once, so redundancy didn't help: the copies failed together. Staged rollouts limit how many machines a bad change reaches before someone notices, and validation at the consumer (keep the last good version) stops it at each machine. More replicas only add more machines to crash.

quiz.q: After a 30-second database hiccup, the payment API stays overloaded for an hour, although the database recovered at once. Clients retry every timeout immediately, up to three times. What is going on, and what helps most?
options: The database is still slow; add read replicas
Coordinated omission is hiding the recovery from the dashboards
A metastable failure kept going by retries; cap retries with a budget and shed work nobody is waiting for
A gray failure; fix the health checks
quiz.why: The hiccup caused timeouts, and each timeout became up to three more requests, so offered load stayed above capacity long after the trigger was gone. Backoff alone only spreads retries out; a retry budget caps how many there are, and shedding work whose callers have given up lets the service drain.

quiz.q: For the average account on a social network, why does fan-out on write do less total work than fan-out on read?
options: Writes are cheaper than reads on every database
Timelines are read far more often than accounts post, and per author the follower count cancels out
The average account has few followers
Fan-out on write skips followers who are offline
quiz.why: Fan-out on write costs one write per follower per post; fan-out on read costs one lookup per follower per read of each follower. The follower count is on both sides, so what decides is posts against reads, and reads win by a wide margin (Twitter served about 60 timeline reads per tweet in 2012). Few followers makes both designs cheap, so it doesn't explain the difference.

quiz.q: Bluesky's 2025 rule gives a user `min(2000 / follows, 1)` of their timeline writes. A user follows 5,000 accounts. What happens?
options: Every post arrives, just later
Only posts from the 2,000 most popular accounts they follow arrive
60% of the posts arrive
About 40% of the posts from the accounts they follow are written into their timeline; the rest are dropped on purpose
quiz.why: 2,000 / 5,000 = 0.4, so each post lands in this user's timeline with probability 0.4, spread across all 5,000 accounts. Nothing is delayed, and popularity doesn't decide which posts survive. The writes are dropped because nobody reads 5,000 accounts' worth of posts anyway, and they made the shards holding such users' timelines hot.

quiz.q: Throughput of a job, measured at 8, 16, 32 and 64 workers, rises and then falls: 64 workers do less than 32. Which part of the Universal Scalability Law must be above zero?
options: β, the coherency cost of every pair of workers keeping in step
Only α, the serial share
Neither: Amdahl's law already explains a fall
The throughput of a single worker
quiz.why: With β = 0 the USL is Amdahl's law, which flattens toward 1 / α but never falls. A fall means some cost grows with the number of worker pairs, such as a shuffle where each worker talks to every other or a lock that wakes every waiter; the curve peaks at √((1 − α) / β).

quiz.q: A Neon compute node running PostgreSQL crashes in the middle of a busy minute. What happens to the transactions it had already committed?
options: They are lost, because the compute node's memory held them
They survive only if the node's local disk can be recovered
They are safe: a commit counts once a quorum of safekeepers has the WAL, and the history lives in object storage
They are rolled back and the clients must retry
quiz.why: Neon separates storage from compute. The compute node is stateless apart from caches; a commit returns only after a quorum of safekeepers has its WAL, and the pageserver and object storage hold the history. A new compute node attaches to the same storage. The local disk is only a cache, which is the question to ask of every such system: where is the durable copy?

quiz.q: You want a page whenever an incident has burned 2% of the month's error budget within an hour, and no page for short blips that burn almost none, however high their error rate. Which rule does that, for a 99.9% SLO?
options: Page when the last 10 minutes are below 99.9%
Page when the error rate is above 1% for 5 minutes
Page when the burn rate is at least 14.4 over the last hour and over the last 5 minutes
Open a ticket when the burn rate is at least 1 over 3 days
quiz.why: A burn rate of 14.4 sustained for an hour spends 14.4 / 720 = 2% of a 30-day budget, and requiring the 5-minute window too makes the page clear soon after the fix. The 10-minute rule pages on blips that cost almost nothing. The 1%-for-5-minutes rule pages on a 3% blip lasting 5 minutes, which uses only about 0.35% of the budget. The 3-day ticket is right for slow leaks, but it can't page within the hour.
